# Write like people speak, and test names in real sentences

Write product copy in active voice and everyday words, and test every name by reading it aloud in the sentences people will actually say.

## Why

External standard, not learned from the user's feedback. Labels and sentences do different jobs: a label is a short noun or verb phrase, and a sentence is how people talk about the product. A name only works if it holds up in both. Active voice shows who does what, and reading aloud catches stiff, formal, or invented phrasing.

## Prefer

- Use active voice, with the actor first: "@A started 3 threads", not "3 threads were started by @A".
- Use contractions and plain verbs, and start statements with the verb when you can.
- Use noun phrases for labels, headings, and badges, and verb plus noun for actions.
- Before choosing a name, draft the sentences users and agents will say with it ("check the lead", "one of its threads is stuck") and keep the name only if they sound natural aloud.

## Avoid

- Passive constructions and weak openers such as "there is" or "you can".
- Prepositional or structural labels that nobody would say aloud.
- Using a product noun as a verb when the verb sounds unnatural.
- Judging a name only as a label, outside the sentences it has to live in.

## Use when

- Writing or reviewing UI copy, notifications, agent messages, and docs.
- Choosing a name for a concept or relationship.

## Do not use when

- A legal, compliance, or technical reference text requires formal wording.

## Sources

- Microsoft Writing Style Guide: Top 10 tips for style and voice — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/style-guide/top-10-tips-style-voice
- Material Design: Writing — https://m1.material.io/style/writing.html
- Grafana Writers' Toolkit: UX writing — https://grafana.com/docs/writers-toolkit/write/style-guide/ux-writing/

## Check

- Does each sentence name its actor before the action?
- Would a person say this sentence aloud, word for word?
- Does the name work as a label and in a spoken sentence?
